newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia loses out in Afghanistan, perhaps Iran too.
newsitem.headline: Russia loses out in Afghanistan, perhaps Iran too.

text.p: The Taleban militia's advance into northern Afghanistan and the outcome of Iran's presidential election have delivered twin setbacks to Russia in a battle for regional influence and control of energy flows out of resource-rich Central Asia, analysts said on Monday.

Russian diplomacy suffered its first blow with the surprise election of moderate Mohammad Khatami as Iran's president, defeating parliamentary speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, who was feted on a visit to Moscow last month and seen in the Kremlin as favouring improved ties with Russia.

Moscow feels a more strategic threat from the Taleban militia's radical brand of Islam, fearing what one Russian official on Monday called a "domino effect" throughout the troubled and nominally Moslem former Soviet states of Central Asia.
"What is happening in Afghanistan could pose a real threat to Tajikistan and Uzbekistan," said Viktor Kremenyuk, an analyst at the USA and Canada Institute in Moscow.
"This is a concern for Russia."
Some regional states have accused Pakistan, the first country to recognise Taleban rule, of backing the militia as part of a drive to forge its way into Central Asian markets.

Following the flight of ousted Afghan president Burhanuddin Rabbani and northern strongman Abdul Rashid Dostum, all that remains of the anti-Taleban alliance, quietly backed by Russia and Iran, is commander Ahmad Shah Masood, said to be holed up somewhere in the fastnesses of the Panjsher Valley.

Russia's first reaction to the fall last weekend of Mazar-i-Sharif and other major northern towns to the Taleban was to put its 20,000 troops stationed in Tajikistan on full alert, ready to march at any time to the Afghan border.

After receiving a bloody mauling at the hands of Afghan guerrilla fighters for a decade following the Soviet invasion of 1979, and with memories of the Chechnya debacle still fresh, the Kremlin is unlikely to go adventuring in Afghanistan.
But Russia still stations forces in Tajikistan to guard the remote border with Afghanistan and carry out peacekeeping duties within the country, itself torn apart by a four-year civil war.
Russia fears any northward march of Islam into its "soft underbelly". So do its Central Asian neighbours.
A Taleban advance had long been expected. But the overnight collapse of the anti-Taleban alliance they backed has sent a wave of panic through the countries of the region.
Central Asian fears are underscored by ethnic divisions in the conflict, with the Taleban, largely Pashtuns from the south, ranged against ethnic Uzbeks and Tajiks in northern Afghanistan.
Andrei Piontkovsky, of the Moscow Centre for Strategic Studies, said the Islamic threat was overplayed. "There is no sign the Taleban is going to export its Islamic ideas."

But Piontkovsky and Russian officials on Monday said the possible arrival of Masood's troops and Afghan refugees in search of sanctuary in Tajikistan could threaten to unravel that country's fragile peace secured last December.
An Afghanistan in the firm grip of Taleban fighters also gives impetus to a once improbable plan to build pipelines from mineral-rich Turkmenistan to Pakistan via Afghanistan.
The pipelines, proposed by U.S. Unocal Corp and Saudi Arabia's Delta Oil, could carry up to 20 billion cubic metres of gas and a year and one million barrels per day of oil.
That would weaken Russia's almost total grip on oil and gas exports from the landlocked ex-Soviet states of Central Asia.

Diplomats say the United States has been quietly pushing the Afghan pipeline in an effort to persuade Central Asian states to bypass Iran, which it accuses of sponsoring terrorist groups, and help break their dependence on Russian-controlled pipelines.
Russia's quest to consolidate alliances following plans by the West's NATO military bloc to expand into eastern Europe has included a determined move to improve ties with Iran.

Pointedly ignoring a renewed bout of western criticism of Tehran over alleged terrorism last month, President Boris Yeltsin received Nateq-Nouri in the Kremlin and said he foresaw strengthening cooperation between Russia and Iran.
The liberal Moscow daily Izvestia said on Monday that Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov's tactic of embracing Nateq-Nouri backfired.
Interfax news agency quoted a Russian foreign ministry official as denying Nateq-Nouri's visit to Moscow had been arranged in the expectation of his becoming president.
But under the headline "Primakov loses elections in Iran, Izvestia said: "Moscow received Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri like a head of state. It was all in vain. The speaker has not become president."
